bull_thesis:
Weis Markets is a debt-free, family-controlled supermarket chain of roughly 200 stores across Pennsylvania and neighbouring states, and the bullish case rests on three things the headline screening data hides.

First, the business inflected in the March 2026 quarter. Revenue rose 4.6% to $1.26 billion, operating profit jumped 64% to $35.7 million, gross margin widened from 24.9% to 26.3% year over year, and earnings per share came in at $1.13 against $0.73. Trailing-twelve-month earnings per share are now $3.99, already ahead of the $3.65 the company earned in all of fiscal 2025. The screener's alarming inputs - a 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple and a gross margin shown as contracting at 22.7% - are both artifacts: the first of a capital-spending cycle, the second of a fiscal-2025 accounting reclassification that shifted roughly $70-80 million of costs from operating expenses into cost of goods sold. On a like-for-like basis margins are widening, not shrinking.

Second, capital allocation has been genuinely excellent. On June 6, 2025 the company bought 2,153,846 shares - 8.0% of itself - from two Weis family trusts for $140 million at $65.00 per share, a 12.3% discount to the previous close and 15.6% below the 30-day average price, funded entirely from cash and marketable securities with no borrowing. A special committee of independent directors negotiated it, Kroll gave a fairness opinion, and the chief executive recused himself from the vote. That single act permanently lifted every remaining shareholder's claim on earnings by about 8%, at a price 13% below where the stock trades today.

Third, there is a credible path to a second such transaction. The selling trusts retained 4,051,383 shares, and on June 1, 2026 the Patricia R. Weis Marital Trust distributed that entire block by will, leaving the trust empty; a third of it went to chief executive Jonathan Weis indirectly. That block is now 16.4% of a company with 24.7 million shares outstanding, held by individuals, in a stock that trades about 73,000 shares a day. It cannot leave through the market. The 2025 deal established both the template and the price mechanism for the company to buy it.

Underneath all of this sits an unusually safe balance sheet: cash and short-term investments of $198.8 million against $173.8 million of lease obligations and no borrowings at all - net cash of about $1.01 per share - with a solvency score of 5.7 and a financial-quality score of 7 out of 9. Most of the store estate is owned outright, which is why net property stands at $1.26 billion, about $51 per share of book value, against a $74.66 share price.

The conditions this case depends on: that the March-quarter margin recovery continues into the August 2026 second-quarter report rather than proving to be a one-quarter comparison effect; that the heavy store-building programme finally levels off, releasing the roughly $80 million a year of capital spending that currently runs above depreciation; and that the family block is retired at a discount rather than dribbled into a thin market.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case is simply that this is an average business at a full price, and that every number people find exciting is either an artifact or already paid for.

Start with returns. Weis earns 5.0% on invested capital and 7.5% on equity. Those are below any reasonable cost of capital, which means each incremental dollar the company puts to work quietly destroys value. And Weis puts a great deal to work: capital spending was $165.6 million in fiscal 2024, $202.4 million in fiscal 2025, and $208.5 million over the last twelve months - 4.16% of sales, against 1.96% at Ingles Markets, 1.83% at Village Super Market and 2.76% at Kroger. Weis spends roughly double its peers' intensity to earn the same or lower returns.

The bull case needs that spending to be a finite programme that ends. Three years of data say the opposite: it has risen every year and was up another 18.5% year over year in the March 2026 quarter. Management has never described it as having an end date, and has never issued guidance of any kind. Until it stops, free cash flow stays near zero - $24.1 million over the last twelve months, a 1.3% yield on the market value, against roughly 9% at Ingles, 8.8% at Village Super Market and 8.1% at Kroger.

What is all that money buying? Comparable-store sales excluding fuel rose 1.2% in the March quarter. That is at or below grocery inflation, which means the basket count is flat to falling. Nearly $210 million a year is buying about one point of same-store growth in a Mid-Atlantic market where Aldi, Lidl and Walmart set the price floor.

The longer arc is not flattering either. Operating profit fell in each of 2023 ($137.2m), 2024 ($131.7m) and 2025 ($102.3m), and fiscal 2025's operating margin of 2.06% closed below the 2.39% Weis earned in 2019, before the pandemic. So this is not purely a windfall unwinding - real margin ground was lost on top of the give-back. Earnings per share went from $4.65 in 2022 to $3.65 in 2025, and a meaningful part of the recovery to $3.99 today comes from the share count falling 8%, not from the stores earning more.

A legislated squeeze is now working through the pharmacy business, which is $672 million of sales, about 14% of the company. Medicare maximum-fair-price rules on ten drugs took effect January 1, 2026 and cost roughly $7.5 million of revenue in the March quarter alone, with further drug cohorts scheduled in later years. This is a permanent haircut to a segment, not a cycle.

And then the relative-value point, which is the sharpest one. The grocery sector has been repriced hard in 2026: Kroger sits 24% below its 52-week high, Albertsons 43% below, Grocery Outlet 51% below. Weis is only 11% off its own high and 5% above its 200-day average. It has simply not participated in the de-rating. Either Weis is the quality survivor of the group, or it is the last name still to reprice - and a 5.0% return on capital with a 1.3% free-cash yield does not support the survivor reading.

Finally, there is no mechanism to force a re-rating even if one were deserved. The Weis family owns about 61%, so no activist can compel anything. There is no analyst coverage, no earnings call, no guidance and no investor day. And the 16.4% block now sitting in individual family hands is as easily an overhang as an opportunity - these are holders who have already demonstrated willingness to sell 12% to 16% below the market price.

What would confirm the bear case: an August 2026 second-quarter report showing capital spending still climbing and comparable sales still around one point; or a family block placed into the market at a discount rather than retired by the company.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not the direction of the story but who has already paid for it.

There is no Wall Street consensus to arbitrage here in the usual sense: no firm in our data vendor's coverage publishes a price target on this listing, the company hosts no earnings call, and it issues no guidance. So the mispricing question is not about analyst assumptions - it is about what the screening machinery and the price tape each believe.

The screening machinery is wrong in the bearish direction, and we correct it: a 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple is an artifact of a capital-spending cycle, not a collapse in earnings power (cash from operations was a healthy $232.6 million over the last twelve months); the 22.7% gross margin shown as contracting is an artifact of a fiscal-2025 cost reclassification, when the like-for-like quarterly margin actually widened from 24.9% to 26.3%; and the flagged 4.08 million shares of insider selling is double-counted and mislabelled - it was 2.15 million shares, and the buyer was the company itself at a 12% discount.

But correcting those errors does not produce an opportunity, because the price tape has already made the same correction. At $74.66 the shares sit 11% below their 52-week high while Kroger is 24% below, Albertsons 43% below and Grocery Outlet 51% below. Weis is being priced as the quality survivor of a de-rating grocery sector. The March-quarter inflection - operating profit up 64%, earnings per share up 55% - is real, and if it repeats through the year Weis earns roughly $4.50 to $4.75 for fiscal 2026. At 16 to 17 times, the peer-median multiple, that is $72 to $81. In other words, the current price already assumes a full-year continuation of the single best quarter this company has printed in three years.

So our genuine disagreement runs the other way: the market is extrapolating one quarter across a business that earns 5.0% on invested capital, converts only 1.3% of its market value into free cash, grows same-store sales below food inflation, and has raised capital spending every year for three years with no stated end. That is not a survivor's profile; it is an average regional grocer trading at a survivor's price.
forcing_function:
There is no hard, dated event that forces a re-rating, and that is a structural feature of this name rather than a temporary gap.

The nearest dated item is the second-quarter earnings release in early August 2026 - the company filed the equivalent quarter on August 6, 2025 - but Weis publishes a two-page press release with no guidance, holds no call, and has no analyst coverage to re-model. A print is a data point, not a forcing function.

The only genuine re-rating mechanism is a second negotiated purchase of the family block, and it is soft in every dimension that matters: no contract, no date, and it requires the three heirs who received the 4,051,383 shares on June 1, 2026 to want to sell. The precedent is strong - the company did exactly this on June 6, 2025 for $140 million at $65.00, with a special committee, a Kroll fairness opinion and the chief executive recused - and the mechanics are well established. If repeated at similar scale it would retire another 8% or so of the company at a discount, adding a low-single-digit percentage to intrinsic value per share. That is worth having; it is not worth paying above fair value to wait for, and there is no way to date it.

The tail scenario, which the estate arithmetic keeps alive, is a sale of the whole company. A century-old family business that has just paid $140 million of estate-driven liquidity and has now distributed the remaining trust holding to three individuals is, structurally, a business working through a generational transfer. Regional grocery has an active consolidation backdrop - Kroger agreed to acquire Giant Eagle in July 2026. But nothing in the filings points to a process, and 61% family ownership means no one outside can start one. This is a possibility to note, not a thesis to size.
valley_of_death:
The risky window over the next three to nine months is not a solvency event - Weis has net cash of about $25 million, no borrowings, a solvency score of 5.7 and no maturity wall of any kind. There is no cash-burn hump and nothing that can force this company's hand. The risk is entirely to the multiple.

The first pressure point is early August 2026, when second-quarter results are due (the company reported the comparable quarter on August 6, 2025). Two lines matter. If capital spending is still climbing - it was up 18.5% year over year in the March quarter, and rose every year from $165.6 million in fiscal 2024 to $208.5 million over the last twelve months - the free-cash normalisation that underpins the bullish case loses another year of credibility. And if comparable-store sales excluding fuel come in around the 1.2% of the March quarter, the volume story stays negative in real terms.

The second is the comparison base itself. The March-quarter earnings jump was flattered by a weak prior-year quarter in which operating profit was only $21.8 million. The comparisons stiffen materially from the September quarter onward, when Weis laps a stronger base.

The third is the pharmacy squeeze compounding. Medicare maximum-fair-price rules cost about $7.5 million of revenue in the March quarter on ten drugs, and further drug cohorts are legislated to follow. That is a recurring, widening drag on 14% of sales.

The fourth is the sector. Grocery multiples have compressed hard through 2026 across Kroger, Albertsons and Grocery Outlet, and Weis has been almost untouched. Mean reversion within a peer group is the most reliable force in equities, and it points the wrong way here.

Set against the current regime: this is one of the few names in the book with genuine independence from the two macro factors the regime document tells us to enforce against - artificial-intelligence capital spending and the oil and Hormuz shock. A defensive food retailer with net cash has almost no exposure to either, and its thesis does not depend on rate cuts, which the regime document explicitly penalises. That independence is a real virtue. It just is not enough to make an expensive stock cheap.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to harvest here, and that cuts both ways.

Weis is not a yield vehicle whose holders would be flushed by a dividend cut - the payout is $1.36 a year, a 1.8% yield covered at about a third of earnings, held at exactly $0.34 a quarter without change since early 2024, on a balance sheet with net cash. Nothing threatens it. The next payment, declared July 16, 2026 with a record date of July 27, is payable August 10; it is a routine quarterly, not a special distribution, and it is not yet paid.

The real positioning fact is the opposite of a washout: it is an overhang. The Weis family owns roughly 61% of the company, and following the June 1, 2026 estate distribution, 4,051,383 shares - 16.4% of the 24.7 million outstanding - now sit in individual family hands rather than in a trust. The stock trades about 73,000 shares on a normal day, so that block represents more than fifty full trading days of volume. It cannot be sold into the market without wrecking the price, which is precisely why the 2025 transaction was structured as a negotiated purchase by the company at a discount.

That structure has an uncomfortable implication for a buyer at $74.66. The known clearing price for a Weis family block is a low-double-digit discount to the prevailing market - 12.3% below the close and 15.6% below the 30-day average in June 2025. Any holder is therefore short an option to a seller with demonstrated price-insensitivity.

On the activist question, which this committee usually tests: it is closed. With 61% family ownership, no outside investor can force a sale, a spin-off, a buyback or a board change. The strategic-process and governance-reset routes that make sum-of-the-parts discounts collectible elsewhere simply do not exist here. Whatever gets done gets done because the family wants it done.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. Weis Markets is a clean, conservative, well-governed little company trading at a price that already reflects its best quarter in three years.

What we found that the screen got wrong is genuinely material, and worth stating because it runs in the company's favour. The 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple is an artifact of a store-building programme, not an earnings collapse - cash from operations was $232.6 million over the last twelve months. The contracting gross margin is an artifact of a fiscal-2025 accounting reclassification; measured like for like, the March-quarter margin widened from 24.9% to 26.3%. And the alarming block of insider selling was not selling at all: on June 6, 2025 the company bought 2,153,846 shares - 8.0% of itself - from two Weis family trusts at $65.00, a 12.3% discount to the prior close, funded from cash, negotiated by a special committee of independent directors with a fairness opinion and the chief executive recused. That is textbook capital allocation, and it permanently lifted every remaining holder's claim on earnings.

But correcting three errors does not create an opportunity when the price has already corrected them. At $74.66 the shares trade at 18.7 times trailing earnings, 7.4 times enterprise value to operating earnings before depreciation, and 1.35 times book value, while the closest regional comparables sit at 6.4 times (Ingles Markets) and 7.3 times (Village Super Market) with free-cash-flow yields near 9% against Weis's 1.3%. More telling still: the grocery sector has been repriced brutally this year - Kroger is 24% below its 52-week high, Albertsons 43% below, Grocery Outlet 51% below - and Weis is 11% off its high and sitting above its 200-day average. Weis is being priced as the survivor of the group on a 5.0% return on invested capital, which is no better than Ingles Markets' 4.7%.

The number I keep returning to is the capital spending. It has risen every year - $165.6 million in fiscal 2024, $202.4 million in fiscal 2025, $208.5 million over the last twelve months, and still up 18.5% year over year in the March quarter - to 4.16% of sales against 1.8% to 2.8% across the peer set. The bullish case requires that to be a finite programme that ends and releases cash. Three years of data say it has not begun to end. And what it is buying is 1.2% comparable-store sales growth, which is below food inflation, meaning basket volumes are flat to falling against Aldi, Lidl and Walmart in the Mid-Atlantic. Spending double your peers' capital intensity, at a 5% return, to hold position, is how a narrow moat erodes slowly - and the operating profit line agrees, falling in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025 to a fiscal-2025 margin below the pre-pandemic 2019 level.

Reconciling the parts gives a base-case value of $67 a share, with an adverse case of $52.50 near book value and a favourable case of $82. The shares trade above the base case. There is no structural floor underneath - net cash is only about $1.01 a share, and the $65.00 paid to the family in 2025 was a one-off negotiated block price, not a standing offer. I have deliberately refused to mark up the owned real estate: the earnings already reflect paying no rent, so a sale-and-leaseback would be close to a wash and treating the property as hidden value double-counts it.

On the current market regime, I give Weis proper credit where it is due. This is one of the genuinely independent names we have looked at - a defensive food retailer with net cash has almost no exposure to the artificial-intelligence capital-spending question or the oil and Hormuz shock, the two shared factors we are told to enforce independence against, and its case does not lean on rate cuts, which the regime penalises. That independence would matter a great deal if the price were right. It is not a reason to overpay.

On the catalyst, I have applied this book's neutrality rule strictly and it changes nothing: the 2025 buyback is spent news, the possible second block purchase is a real but undated and non-binding possibility, and neither is credited or penalised. The verdict rests on the residual value case, and the residual value case is that a competent, honest, average grocer is trading roughly 12% through my estimate of what it is worth, with the wider distance to the downside than to the upside.

What would change my mind, at a named level: the shares at $60 or below - about 1.08 times book value and roughly 15 times trailing earnings - would put the base case comfortably above the price and make the family-block optionality free rather than paid for. Alternatively, an August 2026 report showing capital spending finally flat or falling year over year, alongside comparable-store sales accelerating above 2%, would move the base case up rather than the price down. Absent one of those, this is a name to watch through the August print, not to own into it.

# Weis Markets (WMK) - Forensic Dossier

**Date of this review: July 27, 2026 · Price used: $74.66 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars) · Shares outstanding ~24.74 million · Market value ~$1.85 billion**

## A note on the evidence base

Most companies in this book are interrogated through their earnings calls, where you can watch management's tone shift quarter by quarter and see which analyst questions get dodged. Weis Markets gives you none of that. The paid transcript database we use holds no earnings-call transcript for Weis at all, and every quarterly disclosure I could source - the first-quarter 2026 release on May 6, 2026, the fourth-quarter and full-year 2025 release on March 12, 2026, the second-quarter 2025 release on August 6, 2025 - is a written press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There is no management question-and-answer session on the record, no guidance to hold anyone to, and no sell-side analyst covering the stock with a published price target (our data vendor has no price-target coverage for this listing).

So this dossier interrogates a different evidence trail: the quarterly financial statements, the insider filings (Form 4), the capital-allocation announcements, and the two press releases that carry any management commentary at all. That thinness is itself a finding, and it is scored below.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Weis Markets is a 100-year-old family-controlled supermarket chain based in Sunbury, Pennsylvania, running roughly 200 stores across Pennsylvania, Maryland, New York, New Jersey, West Virginia, Virginia and Delaware. There is no evolving "story" in the usual sense, because management does not tell one. What the record shows instead is a three-act arc visible only in the numbers.

**Act one - the pandemic windfall (2020 to 2022).** Revenue jumped from $3.54 billion in 2019 to $4.70 billion by 2022, and operating profit nearly doubled from $84.6 million to a peak of $163.2 million in 2020. Operating margin - profit from running the stores, as a share of sales - went from 2.39% in 2019 to 3.97% in 2020. Everyone who sold groceries earned like this; it was not a Weis achievement.

**Act two - the give-back (2023 to 2025).** Operating profit fell three years running: $137.2 million, then $131.7 million, then $102.3 million in fiscal 2025. Operating margin landed at 2.06% - *below* the 2.39% Weis earned in 2019, before the pandemic. That last point matters. This was not simply a windfall unwinding; some genuine margin ground was lost on top of it. Earnings per share went from $4.65 in 2022 to $3.65 in 2025.

**Act three - the reset and the inflection (mid-2025 to now).** Two things happened that the fiscal-2025 numbers do not capture. In June 2025 the company retired 8% of its own stock in a single negotiated transaction (detailed in section 7). And in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, reported May 6, the operating line snapped back hard: revenue up 4.6% to $1.26 billion, operating profit up 64% to $35.7 million, earnings per share of $1.13 against $0.73 a year earlier. On a trailing-twelve-month basis (the four quarters through March 28, 2026) earnings per share are now $3.99, already above the $3.65 full-year 2025 figure.

The growth drivers management does name are unglamorous and consistent: store investment and loyalty. Chief Executive Jonathan H. Weis in the May 2026 release: "We continue to invest in broader promotional offerings and enhanced loyalty programs to deliver customer value, while facility and technology investments help manage expenses and improve shopping experiences." And on the scale of the build-out: "In 2025, we delivered 17 large projects, including five new stores, seven major remodels, and five fuel centers, plus over 1,000 smaller facility projects."

Nothing was quietly dropped, because nothing was ever loudly promised.

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

Depreciation, the accounting proxy for wear and tear, is only $126.6 million. Weis is spending 1.65 times what its assets are wearing out. | **Real spending, unproven return.** The spend is verified; the payback is not. |

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, and deliberately uninformative.**

There is no tonal arc to trace because there is no forum in which tone is expressed. Weis issues a two-page press release, states the results, adds two or three sentences of chief-executive commentary that barely change from quarter to quarter, and stops. It has never issued financial guidance in any release I could source. There is no shift from offensive to defensive language because there is almost no language at all.

The one genuine change in register is not verbal - it is behavioural. A company that had not meaningfully repurchased stock in years suddenly deployed $140 million, 7.5% of its market value, on a single day in June 2025. Actions replaced words. That is a confidence signal, but it is one you have to read out of the cash-flow statement rather than out of a transcript.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability score: not assessable - no guidance is given.**

Weis has issued no revenue, earnings, margin or capital-spending guidance that I can locate. There is therefore no promise-versus-delivery record to score, no sandbagging pattern to detect, and no beat rate that means anything (a "beat" against a consensus formed with no company input and effectively no analyst coverage is noise).

What can be scored is *consistency of behaviour*, and here Weis rates well: the dividend has been held at exactly $0.34 per share every single quarter from early 2024 through the one declared July 16, 2026 (record date July 27, payable August 10) - never cut, never raised. The store-project cadence management describes has actually shown up in the capital-spending line. The company does what it says it will do; it just says very little.

The honest caution is that a company with net cash, a 34% payout ratio and no borrowings has held its dividend frozen for more than three years. That is not conservatism so much as inertia.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

There is no earnings call at which anyone could push management. **The estate is the story, and almost nobody is reading it.**

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Not deteriorating - the first quarter of 2026 is a genuine improvement and the buyback was materially value-creating. Groceries are the most defensible corner of physical retail, Weis participates in delivery and pick-up, and 1.2% positive comparable sales is share erosion at a glacial pace, not a collapse. A secondary and legislated pressure sits in the 14% of revenue that is pharmacy, where Medicare maximum-fair-price rules cost about $7.5 million of revenue in the March quarter alone with further drug cohorts scheduled. Neither impairs the terminal value of the business; together they cap what it can ever be worth.

**So is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap? Neither - because it is not cheap.** The apparent bargain in our screener (a 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, a -43% margin of safety) is an artifact of a capital-spending cycle, and once you correct for it the stock lands at a full, unremarkable price for an average-quality regional grocer with net cash and no re-rating engine. # Weis Markets (WMK) - Forensic Dossier

**Date of this review: July 27, 2026 · Price used: $74.66 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars) · Shares outstanding ~24.74 million · Market value ~$1.85 billion**

## A note on the evidence base

Most companies in this book are interrogated through their earnings calls, where you can watch management's tone shift quarter by quarter and see which analyst questions get dodged. Weis Markets gives you none of that. The paid transcript database we use holds no earnings-call transcript for Weis at all, and every quarterly disclosure I could source - the first-quarter 2026 release on May 6, 2026, the fourth-quarter and full-year 2025 release on March 12, 2026, the second-quarter 2025 release on August 6, 2025 - is a written press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There is no management question-and-answer session on the record, no guidance to hold anyone to, and no sell-side analyst covering the stock with a published price target (our data vendor has no price-target coverage for this listing).

So this dossier interrogates a different evidence trail: the quarterly financial statements, the insider filings (Form 4), the capital-allocation announcements, and the two press releases that carry any management commentary at all. That thinness is itself a finding, and it is scored below.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Weis Markets is a 100-year-old family-controlled supermarket chain based in Sunbury, Pennsylvania, running roughly 200 stores across Pennsylvania, Maryland, New York, New Jersey, West Virginia, Virginia and Delaware. There is no evolving "story" in the usual sense, because management does not tell one. What the record shows instead is a three-act arc visible only in the numbers.

**Act one - the pandemic windfall (2020 to 2022).** Revenue jumped from $3.54 billion in 2019 to $4.70 billion by 2022, and operating profit nearly doubled from $84.6 million to a peak of $163.2 million in 2020. Operating margin - profit from running the stores, as a share of sales - went from 2.39% in 2019 to 3.97% in 2020. Everyone who sold groceries earned like this; it was not a Weis achievement.

**Act two - the give-back (2023 to 2025).** Operating profit fell three years running: $137.2 million, then $131.7 million, then $102.3 million in fiscal 2025. Operating margin landed at 2.06% - *below* the 2.39% Weis earned in 2019, before the pandemic. That last point matters. This was not simply a windfall unwinding; some genuine margin ground was lost on top of it. Earnings per share went from $4.65 in 2022 to $3.65 in 2025.

**Act three - the reset and the inflection (mid-2025 to now).** Two things happened that the fiscal-2025 numbers do not capture. In June 2025 the company retired 8% of its own stock in a single negotiated transaction (detailed in section 7). And in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, reported May 6, the operating line snapped back hard: revenue up 4.6% to $1.26 billion, operating profit up 64% to $35.7 million, earnings per share of $1.13 against $0.73 a year earlier. On a trailing-twelve-month basis (the four quarters through March 28, 2026) earnings per share are now $3.99, already above the $3.65 full-year 2025 figure.

The growth drivers management does name are unglamorous and consistent: store investment and loyalty. Chief Executive Jonathan H. Weis in the May 2026 release: "We continue to invest in broader promotional offerings and enhanced loyalty programs to deliver customer value, while facility and technology investments help manage expenses and improve shopping experiences." And on the scale of the build-out: "In 2025, we delivered 17 large projects, including five new stores, seven major remodels, and five fuel centers, plus over 1,000 smaller facility projects."

Nothing was quietly dropped, because nothing was ever loudly promised.

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

Depreciation, the accounting proxy for wear and tear, is only $126.6 million. Weis is spending 1.65 times what its assets are wearing out. | **Real spending, unproven return.** The spend is verified; the payback is not. |

Weis reclassified roughly $70-80 million of costs from operating expenses into cost of goods sold in fiscal 2025 - which is why reported gross profit fell $77 million while reported operating expenses *fell* $47.6 million on 3.5% higher sales, an impossible combination for a grocer facing wage inflation. On a like-for-like quarterly basis gross margin **expanded** from 24.9% to 26.3% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. | **The screener flag is wrong.** Gross margin is expanding, not contracting. |

And they were not sold into the market: **the company itself bought them.** See section 7. | **Refuted.** The single largest "insider sale" in the file is in fact the best capital-allocation decision management has made in a decade. |

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, and deliberately uninformative.**

There is no tonal arc to trace because there is no forum in which tone is expressed. Weis issues a two-page press release, states the results, adds two or three sentences of chief-executive commentary that barely change from quarter to quarter, and stops. It has never issued financial guidance in any release I could source. There is no shift from offensive to defensive language because there is almost no language at all.

The one genuine change in register is not verbal - it is behavioural. A company that had not meaningfully repurchased stock in years suddenly deployed $140 million, 7.5% of its market value, on a single day in June 2025. Actions replaced words. That is a confidence signal, but it is one you have to read out of the cash-flow statement rather than out of a transcript.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability score: not assessable - no guidance is given.**

Weis has issued no revenue, earnings, margin or capital-spending guidance that I can locate. There is therefore no promise-versus-delivery record to score, no sandbagging pattern to detect, and no beat rate that means anything (a "beat" against a consensus formed with no company input and effectively no analyst coverage is noise).

What can be scored is *consistency of behaviour*, and here Weis rates well: the dividend has been held at exactly $0.34 per share every single quarter from early 2024 through the one declared July 16, 2026 (record date July 27, payable August 10) - never cut, never raised. The store-project cadence management describes has actually shown up in the capital-spending line. The company does what it says it will do; it just says very little.

The honest caution is that a company with net cash, a 34% payout ratio and no borrowings has held its dividend frozen for more than three years. That is not conservatism so much as inertia.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

There are effectively none, and that is the point. No sell-side firm publishes a price target on this listing in our data vendor's coverage. There is no earnings call at which anyone could push management. The only outside voice in the file is a May 20, 2026 note on a retail research platform arguing the "premiumisation" story lifted gross margin to 26.3% while flagging that Inflation Reduction Act drug-pricing rules pressure the pharmacy business - and it rates the stock a hold at roughly fair value.

The questions nobody is asking, which a committee should ask:

1. **When does the building stop?** Capital spending has risen for three consecutive years and was still up 18.5% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. Management has never framed it as a finite programme with an end date. Until it ends, reported free cash flow stays near zero.
2. **What is the return on all of it?** Roughly $575 million spent over three years has produced same-store sales growth of about one point and a return on invested capital of 5%.
3. **What happens to the remaining family block?** Detailed in section 7.
4. **How deep does the pharmacy squeeze go?** The first quarter carried a $7.5 million revenue headwind from Medicare maximum-fair-price rules on ten drugs effective January 1, 2026. Further drug cohorts are legislated to follow. Pharmacy is $672 million of sales, about 14% of the business.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Capital spending is accelerating, not normalising** (fiscal 2024 $165.6m, fiscal 2025 $202.4m, first quarter 2026 up another 18.5%). The bullish case rests on this rolling off. Three years of data say it is not rolling off.
- **Reinvestment below the cost of capital.** A 5.0% return on invested capital, with capital spending at 4.16% of sales against peer intensity of 1.8% to 2.8%, is the textbook profile of value leaking away slowly.
- **Same-store sales below food inflation** (+1.2% excluding fuel, first quarter 2026) means basket volume is flat to falling in a Mid-Atlantic market where Aldi, Lidl and Walmart set the price floor.
- **Fiscal 2025 operating margin of 2.06% sits below the pre-pandemic 2.39% of 2019.** Some of the earnings decline is a pandemic windfall unwinding, but not all of it.
- **A cost reclassification in fiscal 2025** moved roughly $70-80 million between cost of goods sold and operating expenses, breaking the comparability of reported gross margin. Not deceptive, but it has corrupted at least one screening input.
- **Legislated pharmacy reimbursement compression**, first bite $7.5 million in the March quarter, with further waves scheduled.
- **Effectively no disclosure infrastructure**: no calls, no guidance, no analyst coverage. Nothing forces this company to explain itself.

**Green flags**

- **The June 6, 2025 buyback is genuinely excellent.** 2,153,846 shares - 8.0% of the company - retired at $65.00 for $140 million, a 12.3% discount to the prior close and 15.6% below the 30-day average price, funded entirely from cash and securities on hand with no borrowing.
- **The governance around it was textbook.** A special committee of independent directors negotiated and recommended it, Kroll provided a fairness opinion, and Jonathan Weis recused himself from the board vote. For a company where the family owns roughly 61%, that is the right way to buy stock from the family.
- **A real first-quarter 2026 inflection**: operating profit up 64%, gross margin up about 140 basis points year over year, earnings per share up 55%.
- **Genuine balance-sheet strength**: net cash, no borrowings, a solvency score of 5.7 and a quality score of 7 of 9.
- **Small but real open-market insider buying**: the chief operating officer bought 500 shares at $65.51 on November 7, 2025, adding to purchases in 2024 and 2023. Small sums, but bought with his own money at prices below today's.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The estate is the story, and almost nobody is reading it.**

Two filings, fourteen months apart, describe a single unfolding process:

- **June 6, 2025.** The company bought 2,153,846 shares for $140 million at $65.00 from the Patricia R. Weis Marital Trust and the Patricia G. Ross Weis Revocable Trust. The purpose, per the announcement, was to help meet estate-tax obligations. After it, "members of the Weis Family remain owners of approximately 61% of the outstanding Common Stock," and the selling trusts retained **4,051,383 shares**.
- **June 1, 2026.** A Form 4 filed June 4 shows the Patricia R. Weis Marital Trust distributing its entire remaining holding - **exactly those 4,051,383 shares** - by will and the laws of descent, leaving the trust at zero. Jonathan Weis, signing as trustee, reports acquiring 1,350,461 of them indirectly, precisely one third. The block has moved from one trust into (by arithmetic) three individual estates.

That block is now 16.4% of a company with only 24.7 million shares outstanding, sitting in individual hands, in a stock that trades about 73,000 shares on a normal day. It would take more than fifty trading days to sell through the market. There are only two realistic exits: another negotiated purchase by the company, or a strategic sale of the whole business. The 2025 transaction established the template, the price mechanism (a low-double-digit discount to market) and the governance process for the first of those.

This is the single most important thing in the file, and it is genuinely two-sided. It is a potential source of accretive per-share value - and it is a 16.4% overhang in a thinly traded stock whose holders have a demonstrated willingness to sell below market.

**A second, quieter signal.** Weis funded the 2025 buyback by selling marketable securities. Short-term investments went from $155.2 million in September 2025 to $101.1 million in March 2026 while cash rose. The company is progressively converting its investment portfolio into operating and transactional capacity. That is consistent with preparing for something, though it is equally consistent with simply funding the store programme.

**On the real estate.** Weis owns most of its stores outright - which is why it carries $1.26 billion of net property against only $174 million of lease obligations, mostly finance leases. It is tempting to mark that property to market and call the difference upside. Resist it. The earnings already reflect paying no rent; sell the property in a sale-and-leaseback at a 7% yield and you would raise real cash but hand back roughly $130 million a year of rent against $246 million of trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The property value is a downside floor, not upside. Anyone presenting it as a hidden asset is double-counting.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Not deteriorating - the first quarter of 2026 is a genuine improvement and the buyback was materially value-creating. Not strengthening - the underlying franchise is growing sales at roughly the rate of inflation, earning 5% on capital, and spending nearly twice its peers' capital intensity to hold position.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing: the market is already paying for the inflection.** At $74.66 the stock trades at 18.7 times trailing earnings, 7.4 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and 1.35 times book value - while the closest comparable regional grocers trade at 6.4 times (Ingles Markets) and 7.3 times (Village Super Market) with free-cash-flow yields near 9% against Weis's 1.3%. Meanwhile the wider grocery group has been repriced brutally in 2026 - Kroger is 24% below its 52-week high, Albertsons 43% below, Grocery Outlet 51% below - and Weis is only 11% off its own high, sitting 5% above its 200-day average. Weis has not participated in a sector de-rating. Either it is the quality survivor, or it is the last one still to reprice. On a 5.0% return on capital and a 1.3% free-cash yield, the numbers do not support the survivor reading.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and the trend is eroding.** The moat type is local scale-cost advantage reinforced by owned real estate - in small and mid-size Pennsylvania towns, being the established full-service supermarket with a paid-for building is a real barrier, and Weis has held it for a century. But width is measured by returns, and Weis earns 5.0% on invested capital while spending 4.16% of sales to stand still. Operating profit fell in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and fiscal 2025's margin closed below the pre-pandemic 2019 level. One strong quarter does not reverse that arc; it makes the arc worth watching.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is the retail channel shift - hard discounters (Aldi, Lidl) and Walmart taking share of the grocery basket, with online grocery a slower third pressure. Groceries are the most defensible corner of physical retail, Weis participates in delivery and pick-up, and 1.2% positive comparable sales is share erosion at a glacial pace, not a collapse. A secondary and legislated pressure sits in the 14% of revenue that is pharmacy, where Medicare maximum-fair-price rules cost about $7.5 million of revenue in the March quarter alone with further drug cohorts scheduled. Neither impairs the terminal value of the business; together they cap what it can ever be worth.

**So is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap? Neither - because it is not cheap.** The apparent bargain in our screener (a 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, a -43% margin of safety) is an artifact of a capital-spending cycle, and once you correct for it the stock lands at a full, unremarkable price for an average-quality regional grocer with net cash and no re-rating engine. The forensic quality is clean; the entry price is not.

interrogator_dossier:
# Weis Markets (WMK) - Forensic Dossier

**Date of this review: July 27, 2026 · Price used: $74.66 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars) · Shares outstanding ~24.74 million · Market value ~$1.85 billion**

## A note on the evidence base

Most companies in this book are interrogated through their earnings calls, where you can watch management's tone shift quarter by quarter and see which analyst questions get dodged. Weis Markets gives you none of that. The paid transcript database we use holds no earnings-call transcript for Weis at all, and every quarterly disclosure I could source - the first-quarter 2026 release on May 6, 2026, the fourth-quarter and full-year 2025 release on March 12, 2026, the second-quarter 2025 release on August 6, 2025 - is a written press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There is no management question-and-answer session on the record, no guidance to hold anyone to, and no sell-side analyst covering the stock with a published price target (our data vendor has no price-target coverage for this listing).

So this dossier interrogates a different evidence trail: the quarterly financial statements, the insider filings (Form 4), the capital-allocation announcements, and the two press releases that carry any management commentary at all. That thinness is itself a finding, and it is scored below.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Weis Markets is a 100-year-old family-controlled supermarket chain based in Sunbury, Pennsylvania, running roughly 200 stores across Pennsylvania, Maryland, New York, New Jersey, West Virginia, Virginia and Delaware. There is no evolving "story" in the usual sense, because management does not tell one. What the record shows instead is a three-act arc visible only in the numbers.

**Act one - the pandemic windfall (2020 to 2022).** Revenue jumped from $3.54 billion in 2019 to $4.70 billion by 2022, and operating profit nearly doubled from $84.6 million to a peak of $163.2 million in 2020. Operating margin - profit from running the stores, as a share of sales - went from 2.39% in 2019 to 3.97% in 2020. Everyone who sold groceries earned like this; it was not a Weis achievement.

**Act two - the give-back (2023 to 2025).** Operating profit fell three years running: $137.2 million, then $131.7 million, then $102.3 million in fiscal 2025. Operating margin landed at 2.06% - *below* the 2.39% Weis earned in 2019, before the pandemic. That last point matters. This was not simply a windfall unwinding; some genuine margin ground was lost on top of it. Earnings per share went from $4.65 in 2022 to $3.65 in 2025.

**Act three - the reset and the inflection (mid-2025 to now).** Two things happened that the fiscal-2025 numbers do not capture. In June 2025 the company retired 8% of its own stock in a single negotiated transaction (detailed in section 7). And in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, reported May 6, the operating line snapped back hard: revenue up 4.6% to $1.26 billion, operating profit up 64% to $35.7 million, earnings per share of $1.13 against $0.73 a year earlier. On a trailing-twelve-month basis (the four quarters through March 28, 2026) earnings per share are now $3.99, already above the $3.65 full-year 2025 figure.

The growth drivers management does name are unglamorous and consistent: store investment and loyalty. Chief Executive Jonathan H. Weis in the May 2026 release: "We continue to invest in broader promotional offerings and enhanced loyalty programs to deliver customer value, while facility and technology investments help manage expenses and improve shopping experiences." And on the scale of the build-out: "In 2025, we delivered 17 large projects, including five new stores, seven major remodels, and five fuel centers, plus over 1,000 smaller facility projects."

Nothing was quietly dropped, because nothing was ever loudly promised.

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim / market perception | What the numbers actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy store investment "helps manage expenses and improve shopping experiences" (May 2026) | Capital spending has gone from $165.6 million in fiscal 2024 to $202.4 million in fiscal 2025 to $208.5 million over the last twelve months - 4.16% of sales. Depreciation, the accounting proxy for wear and tear, is only $126.6 million. Weis is spending 1.65 times what its assets are wearing out. | **Real spending, unproven return.** The spend is verified; the payback is not. |
| The investment is winning customers | Comparable-store sales excluding fuel rose just 1.2% in the first quarter of 2026 (2.2% on a two-year stacked basis). That is at or below grocery inflation, which means flat-to-down basket volume. | **Diverges.** Nearly $210 million a year of spending is buying roughly one point of same-store growth. |
| Weis is a high-quality regional grocer | Return on invested capital - the profit earned on every dollar of capital put to work - is 5.0%. Return on equity is 7.5%. Both sit below any sensible cost of capital, and below where they were five years ago. | **Poorer than the narrative.** This is a business reinvesting heavily at returns that do not clear the bar. |
| Gross margin is contracting (as our own screener flags at 22.7%) | This is a bookkeeping artifact. Weis reclassified roughly $70-80 million of costs from operating expenses into cost of goods sold in fiscal 2025 - which is why reported gross profit fell $77 million while reported operating expenses *fell* $47.6 million on 3.5% higher sales, an impossible combination for a grocer facing wage inflation. On a like-for-like quarterly basis gross margin **expanded** from 24.9% to 26.3% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. | **The screener flag is wrong.** Gross margin is expanding, not contracting. |
| Free cash flow has collapsed 81.5% (screener) and the stock trades at 390 times free cash flow | Directionally true and worth taking seriously, but it is a capital-spending artifact, not an earnings collapse. Cash from operations over the last twelve months was a healthy $232.6 million. Subtract $208.5 million of capital spending and only $24.1 million of free cash is left. | **True but misread.** The cash engine works; management is spending nearly all of it. |
| The balance sheet is conservative | Verified. Cash and short-term investments of $198.8 million against $173.8 million of lease-related debt and no borrowings at all: **net cash of $25.1 million**, about $1.01 per share. Altman-Z solvency score 5.7, Piotroski quality score 7 of 9. | **Matches, and then some.** |
| Insider selling is a warning (screener shows 3 sells totalling 4,075,592 shares) | This is double-counted and badly mislabelled. The same 2,153,846 shares were reported twice - once by the selling trust and once by its beneficial owner. And they were not sold into the market: **the company itself bought them.** See section 7. | **Refuted.** The single largest "insider sale" in the file is in fact the best capital-allocation decision management has made in a decade. |

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, and deliberately uninformative.**

There is no tonal arc to trace because there is no forum in which tone is expressed. Weis issues a two-page press release, states the results, adds two or three sentences of chief-executive commentary that barely change from quarter to quarter, and stops. It has never issued financial guidance in any release I could source. There is no shift from offensive to defensive language because there is almost no language at all.

The one genuine change in register is not verbal - it is behavioural. A company that had not meaningfully repurchased stock in years suddenly deployed $140 million, 7.5% of its market value, on a single day in June 2025. Actions replaced words. That is a confidence signal, but it is one you have to read out of the cash-flow statement rather than out of a transcript.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability score: not assessable - no guidance is given.**

Weis has issued no revenue, earnings, margin or capital-spending guidance that I can locate. There is therefore no promise-versus-delivery record to score, no sandbagging pattern to detect, and no beat rate that means anything (a "beat" against a consensus formed with no company input and effectively no analyst coverage is noise).

What can be scored is *consistency of behaviour*, and here Weis rates well: the dividend has been held at exactly $0.34 per share every single quarter from early 2024 through the one declared July 16, 2026 (record date July 27, payable August 10) - never cut, never raised. The store-project cadence management describes has actually shown up in the capital-spending line. The company does what it says it will do; it just says very little.

The honest caution is that a company with net cash, a 34% payout ratio and no borrowings has held its dividend frozen for more than three years. That is not conservatism so much as inertia.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

There are effectively none, and that is the point. No sell-side firm publishes a price target on this listing in our data vendor's coverage. There is no earnings call at which anyone could push management. The only outside voice in the file is a May 20, 2026 note on a retail research platform arguing the "premiumisation" story lifted gross margin to 26.3% while flagging that Inflation Reduction Act drug-pricing rules pressure the pharmacy business - and it rates the stock a hold at roughly fair value.

The questions nobody is asking, which a committee should ask:

1. **When does the building stop?** Capital spending has risen for three consecutive years and was still up 18.5% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. Management has never framed it as a finite programme with an end date. Until it ends, reported free cash flow stays near zero.
2. **What is the return on all of it?** Roughly $575 million spent over three years has produced same-store sales growth of about one point and a return on invested capital of 5%.
3. **What happens to the remaining family block?** Detailed in section 7.
4. **How deep does the pharmacy squeeze go?** The first quarter carried a $7.5 million revenue headwind from Medicare maximum-fair-price rules on ten drugs effective January 1, 2026. Further drug cohorts are legislated to follow. Pharmacy is $672 million of sales, about 14% of the business.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Capital spending is accelerating, not normalising** (fiscal 2024 $165.6m, fiscal 2025 $202.4m, first quarter 2026 up another 18.5%). The bullish case rests on this rolling off. Three years of data say it is not rolling off.
- **Reinvestment below the cost of capital.** A 5.0% return on invested capital, with capital spending at 4.16% of sales against peer intensity of 1.8% to 2.8%, is the textbook profile of value leaking away slowly.
- **Same-store sales below food inflation** (+1.2% excluding fuel, first quarter 2026) means basket volume is flat to falling in a Mid-Atlantic market where Aldi, Lidl and Walmart set the price floor.
- **Fiscal 2025 operating margin of 2.06% sits below the pre-pandemic 2.39% of 2019.** Some of the earnings decline is a pandemic windfall unwinding, but not all of it.
- **A cost reclassification in fiscal 2025** moved roughly $70-80 million between cost of goods sold and operating expenses, breaking the comparability of reported gross margin. Not deceptive, but it has corrupted at least one screening input.
- **Legislated pharmacy reimbursement compression**, first bite $7.5 million in the March quarter, with further waves scheduled.
- **Effectively no disclosure infrastructure**: no calls, no guidance, no analyst coverage. Nothing forces this company to explain itself.

**Green flags**

- **The June 6, 2025 buyback is genuinely excellent.** 2,153,846 shares - 8.0% of the company - retired at $65.00 for $140 million, a 12.3% discount to the prior close and 15.6% below the 30-day average price, funded entirely from cash and securities on hand with no borrowing.
- **The governance around it was textbook.** A special committee of independent directors negotiated and recommended it, Kroll provided a fairness opinion, and Jonathan Weis recused himself from the board vote. For a company where the family owns roughly 61%, that is the right way to buy stock from the family.
- **A real first-quarter 2026 inflection**: operating profit up 64%, gross margin up about 140 basis points year over year, earnings per share up 55%.
- **Genuine balance-sheet strength**: net cash, no borrowings, a solvency score of 5.7 and a quality score of 7 of 9.
- **Small but real open-market insider buying**: the chief operating officer bought 500 shares at $65.51 on November 7, 2025, adding to purchases in 2024 and 2023. Small sums, but bought with his own money at prices below today's.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The estate is the story, and almost nobody is reading it.**

Two filings, fourteen months apart, describe a single unfolding process:

- **June 6, 2025.** The company bought 2,153,846 shares for $140 million at $65.00 from the Patricia R. Weis Marital Trust and the Patricia G. Ross Weis Revocable Trust. The purpose, per the announcement, was to help meet estate-tax obligations. After it, "members of the Weis Family remain owners of approximately 61% of the outstanding Common Stock," and the selling trusts retained **4,051,383 shares**.
- **June 1, 2026.** A Form 4 filed June 4 shows the Patricia R. Weis Marital Trust distributing its entire remaining holding - **exactly those 4,051,383 shares** - by will and the laws of descent, leaving the trust at zero. Jonathan Weis, signing as trustee, reports acquiring 1,350,461 of them indirectly, precisely one third. The block has moved from one trust into (by arithmetic) three individual estates.

That block is now 16.4% of a company with only 24.7 million shares outstanding, sitting in individual hands, in a stock that trades about 73,000 shares on a normal day. It would take more than fifty trading days to sell through the market. There are only two realistic exits: another negotiated purchase by the company, or a strategic sale of the whole business. The 2025 transaction established the template, the price mechanism (a low-double-digit discount to market) and the governance process for the first of those.

This is the single most important thing in the file, and it is genuinely two-sided. It is a potential source of accretive per-share value - and it is a 16.4% overhang in a thinly traded stock whose holders have a demonstrated willingness to sell below market.

**A second, quieter signal.** Weis funded the 2025 buyback by selling marketable securities. Short-term investments went from $155.2 million in September 2025 to $101.1 million in March 2026 while cash rose. The company is progressively converting its investment portfolio into operating and transactional capacity. That is consistent with preparing for something, though it is equally consistent with simply funding the store programme.

**On the real estate.** Weis owns most of its stores outright - which is why it carries $1.26 billion of net property against only $174 million of lease obligations, mostly finance leases. It is tempting to mark that property to market and call the difference upside. Resist it. The earnings already reflect paying no rent; sell the property in a sale-and-leaseback at a 7% yield and you would raise real cash but hand back roughly $130 million a year of rent against $246 million of trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The property value is a downside floor, not upside. Anyone presenting it as a hidden asset is double-counting.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Not deteriorating - the first quarter of 2026 is a genuine improvement and the buyback was materially value-creating. Not strengthening - the underlying franchise is growing sales at roughly the rate of inflation, earning 5% on capital, and spending nearly twice its peers' capital intensity to hold position.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing: the market is already paying for the inflection.** At $74.66 the stock trades at 18.7 times trailing earnings, 7.4 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and 1.35 times book value - while the closest comparable regional grocers trade at 6.4 times (Ingles Markets) and 7.3 times (Village Super Market) with free-cash-flow yields near 9% against Weis's 1.3%. Meanwhile the wider grocery group has been repriced brutally in 2026 - Kroger is 24% below its 52-week high, Albertsons 43% below, Grocery Outlet 51% below - and Weis is only 11% off its own high, sitting 5% above its 200-day average. Weis has not participated in a sector de-rating. Either it is the quality survivor, or it is the last one still to reprice. On a 5.0% return on capital and a 1.3% free-cash yield, the numbers do not support the survivor reading.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and the trend is eroding.** The moat type is local scale-cost advantage reinforced by owned real estate - in small and mid-size Pennsylvania towns, being the established full-service supermarket with a paid-for building is a real barrier, and Weis has held it for a century. But width is measured by returns, and Weis earns 5.0% on invested capital while spending 4.16% of sales to stand still. Operating profit fell in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and fiscal 2025's margin closed below the pre-pandemic 2019 level. One strong quarter does not reverse that arc; it makes the arc worth watching.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is the retail channel shift - hard discounters (Aldi, Lidl) and Walmart taking share of the grocery basket, with online grocery a slower third pressure. Groceries are the most defensible corner of physical retail, Weis participates in delivery and pick-up, and 1.2% positive comparable sales is share erosion at a glacial pace, not a collapse. A secondary and legislated pressure sits in the 14% of revenue that is pharmacy, where Medicare maximum-fair-price rules cost about $7.5 million of revenue in the March quarter alone with further drug cohorts scheduled. Neither impairs the terminal value of the business; together they cap what it can ever be worth.

**So is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap? Neither - because it is not cheap.** The apparent bargain in our screener (a 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple, a -43% margin of safety) is an artifact of a capital-spending cycle, and once you correct for it the stock lands at a full, unremarkable price for an average-quality regional grocer with net cash and no re-rating engine. The forensic quality is clean; the entry price is not.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: ERODING | SECULAR_THREAT: material

Those are below any reasonable cost of capital, which means each incremental dollar the company puts to work quietly destroys value. And Weis puts a great deal to work: capital spending was $165.6 million in fiscal 2024, $202.4 million in fiscal 2025, and $208.5 million over the last twelve months - 4.16% of sales, against 1.96% at Ingles Markets, 1.83% at Village Super Market and 2.76% at Kroger. Weis spends roughly double its peers' intensity to earn the same or lower returns.

The bull case needs that spending to be a finite programme that ends. Three years of data say the opposite: it has risen every year and was up another 18.5% year over year in the March 2026 quarter. Management has never described it as having an end date, and has never issued guidance of any kind. Until it stops, free cash flow stays near zero - $24.1 million over the last twelve months, a 1.3% yield on the market value, against roughly 9% at Ingles, 8.8% at Village Super Market and 8.1% at Kroger.

What is all that money buying? Comparable-store sales excluding fuel rose 1.2% in the March quarter. That is at or below grocery inflation, which means the basket count is flat to falling. Nearly $210 million a year is buying about one point of same-store growth in a Mid-Atlantic market where Aldi, Lidl and Walmart set the price floor.

The longer arc is not flattering either. Operating profit fell in each of 2023 ($137.2m), 2024 ($131.7m) and 2025 ($102.3m), and fiscal 2025's operating margin of 2.06% closed below the 2.39% Weis earned in 2019, before the pandemic. So this is not purely a windfall unwinding - real margin ground was lost on top of the give-back. Earnings per share went from $4.65 in 2022 to $3.65 in 2025, and a meaningful part of the recovery to $3.99 today comes from the share count falling 8%, not from the stores earning more.

A legislated squeeze is now working through the pharmacy business, which is $672 million of sales, about 14% of the company. Medicare maximum-fair-price rules on ten drugs took effect January 1, 2026 and cost roughly $7.5 million of revenue in the March quarter alone, with further drug cohorts scheduled in later years. This is a permanent haircut to a segment, not a cycle.

And then the relative-value point, which is the sharpest one. The grocery sector has been repriced hard in 2026: Kroger sits 24% below its 52-week high, Albertsons 43% below, Grocery Outlet 51% below. Weis is only 11% off its own high and 5% above its 200-day average. It has simply not participated in the de-rating. Either Weis is the quality survivor of the group, or it is the last name still to reprice - and a 5.0% return on capital with a 1.3% free-cash yield does not support the survivor reading.

Finally, there is no mechanism to force a re-rating even if one were deserved. The Weis family owns about 61%, so no activist can compel anything. There is no analyst coverage, no earnings call, no guidance and no investor day. And the 16.4% block now sitting in individual family hands is as easily an overhang as an opportunity - these are holders who have already demonstrated willingness to sell 12% to 16% below the market price.

What would confirm the bear case: an August 2026 second-quarter report showing capital spending still climbing and comparable sales still around one point; or a family block placed into the market at a discount rather than retired by the company.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not the direction of the story but who has already paid for it.

There is no Wall Street consensus to arbitrage here in the usual sense: no firm in our data vendor's coverage publishes a price target on this listing, the company hosts no earnings call, and it issues no guidance. So the mispricing question is not about analyst assumptions - it is about what the screening machinery and the price tape each believe.

The screening machinery is wrong in the bearish direction, and we correct it: a 390-times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple is an artifact of a capital-spending cycle, not a collapse in earnings power (cash from operations was a healthy $232.6 million over the last twelve months); the 22.7% gross margin shown as contracting is an artifact of a fiscal-2025 cost reclassification, when the like-for-like quarterly margin actually widened from 24.9% to 26.3%; and the flagged 4.08 million shares of insider selling is double-counted and mislabelled - it was 2.15 million shares, and the buyer was the company itself at a 12% discount.

But correcting those errors does not produce an opportunity, because the price tape has already made the same correction. At $74.66 the shares sit 11% below their 52-week high while Kroger is 24% below, Albertsons 43% below and Grocery Outlet 51% below. The March-quarter inflection - operating profit up 64%, earnings per share up 55% - is real, and if it repeats through the year Weis earns roughly $4.50 to $4.75 for fiscal 2026. At 16 to 17 times, the peer-median multiple, that is $72 to $81. In other words, the current price already assumes a full-year continuation of the single best quarter this company has printed in three years.

So our genuine disagreement runs the other way: the market is extrapolating one quarter across a business that earns 5.0% on invested capital, converts only 1.3% of its market value into free cash, grows same-store sales below food inflation, and has raised capital spending every year for three years with no stated end. That is not a survivor's profile; it is an average regional grocer trading at a survivor's price.
forcing_function:
There is no hard, dated event that forces a re-rating, and that is a structural feature of this name rather than a temporary gap.

The nearest dated item is the second-quarter earnings release in early August 2026 - the company filed the equivalent quarter on August 6, 2025 - but Weis publishes a two-page press release with no guidance, holds no call, and has no analyst coverage to re-model. The precedent is strong - the company did exactly this on June 6, 2025 for $140 million at $65.00, with a special committee, a Kroll fairness opinion and the chief executive recused - and the mechanics are well established. If repeated at similar scale it would retire another 8% or so of the company at a discount, adding a low-single-digit percentage to intrinsic value per share. That is worth having; it is not worth paying above fair value to wait for, and there is no way to date it.

The tail scenario, which the estate arithmetic keeps alive, is a sale of the whole company. valley_of_death:
The risky window over the next three to nine months is not a solvency event - Weis has net cash of about $25 million, no borrowings, a solvency score of 5.7 and no maturity wall of any kind. The fourth is the sector. Grocery multiples have compressed hard through 2026 across Kroger, Albertsons and Grocery Outlet, and Weis has been almost untouched. Mean reversion within a peer group is the most reliable force in equities, and it points the wrong way here.

Set against the current regime: this is one of the few names in the book with genuine independence from the two macro factors the regime document tells us to enforce against - artificial-intelligence capital spending and the oil and Hormuz shock. A defensive food retailer with net cash has almost no exposure to either, and its thesis does not depend on rate cuts, which the regime document explicitly penalises. That independence is a real virtue. It just is not enough to make an expensive stock cheap.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to harvest here, and that cuts both ways.

Weis is not a yield vehicle whose holders would be flushed by a dividend cut - the payout is $1.36 a year, a 1.8% yield covered at about a third of earnings, held at exactly $0.34 a quarter without change since early 2024, on a balance sheet with net cash. Nothing threatens it. The next payment, declared July 16, 2026 with a record date of July 27, is payable August 10; it is a routine quarterly, not a special distribution, and it is not yet paid.

The Weis family owns roughly 61% of the company, and following the June 1, 2026 estate distribution, 4,051,383 shares - 16.4% of the 24.7 million outstanding - now sit in individual family hands rather than in a trust. The stock trades about 73,000 shares on a normal day, so that block represents more than fifty full trading days of volume. It cannot be sold into the market without wrecking the price, which is precisely why the 2025 transaction was structured as a negotiated purchase by the company at a discount.

That structure has an uncomfortable implication for a buyer at $74.66. The known clearing price for a Weis family block is a low-double-digit discount to the prevailing market - 12.3% below the close and 15.6% below the 30-day average in June 2025. Any holder is therefore short an option to a seller with demonstrated price-insensitivity.

The strategic-process and governance-reset routes that make sum-of-the-parts discounts collectible elsewhere simply do not exist here. Whatever gets done gets done because the family wants it done.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. Weis Markets is a clean, conservative, well-governed little company trading at a price that already reflects its best quarter in three years.

What we found that the screen got wrong is genuinely material, and worth stating because it runs in the company's favour. The number I keep returning to is the capital spending. It has risen every year - $165.6 million in fiscal 2024, $202.4 million in fiscal 2025, $208.5 million over the last twelve months, and still up 18.5% year over year in the March quarter - to 4.16% of sales against 1.8% to 2.8% across the peer set. And what it is buying is 1.2% comparable-store sales growth, which is below food inflation, meaning basket volumes are flat to falling against Aldi, Lidl and Walmart in the Mid-Atlantic. There is no structural floor underneath - net cash is only about $1.01 a share, and the $65.00 paid to the family in 2025 was a one-off negotiated block price, not a standing offer. I have deliberately refused to mark up the owned real estate: the earnings already reflect paying no rent, so a sale-and-leaseback would be close to a wash and treating the property as hidden value double-counts it.

This is one of the genuinely independent names we have looked at - a defensive food retailer with net cash has almost no exposure to the artificial-intelligence capital-spending question or the oil and Hormuz shock, the two shared factors we are told to enforce independence against, and its case does not lean on rate cuts, which the regime penalises.
